answers.brief_reasoning: Lower relative interest rates make Moravian assets less attractive: foreigners demand fewer kets (D shifts left), and Moravians supply more kets to buy foreign assets (S shifts right). Either shift, or both, gives a lower ER2.
answers.final_answer: Demand for the ket shifts left (and/or supply shifts right), so the new rate ER2 is below ER1.

answers.brief_reasoning: The exchange rate falls from ER1 to ER2.
answers.final_answer: The ket depreciates (its value falls).

answers.brief_reasoning: Financial capital flows to wherever the return is higher.
answers.final_answer: With lower interest rates, Moravian financial assets earn a lower return than foreign assets. Foreign investors buy fewer Moravian assets, so they demand fewer kets. Moravian investors buy more foreign assets, so they supply more kets to get foreign currency.

answers.brief_reasoning: Depreciation makes Moravian goods cheaper for foreigners and foreign goods dearer for Moravians, so exports rise and imports fall.
answers.final_answer: A weaker ket makes Moravian exports cheaper for foreign buyers and imports more expensive for Moravians, so exports rise, imports fall and net exports increase. Net exports are part of aggregate demand, so AD shifts right and real GDP rises in the short run.

answers.brief_reasoning: Axes: inflation rate (vertical), unemployment rate (horizontal). LRPC is vertical at 6%. SRPC slopes downward and crosses the LRPC at 6% unemployment and 3% inflation. Label that crossing point as the initial long-run equilibrium.
answers.final_answer: Vertical LRPC at 6% unemployment; downward-sloping SRPC1 crossing it at (6%, 3%), the labeled equilibrium point.

answers.brief_reasoning: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC up (to the right). SRPC2 crosses the LRPC at 6% unemployment and an inflation rate above 3%.

answers.brief_reasoning: Long-run unemployment equals the natural rate, so it is unaffected by expected inflation.
answers.final_answer: No change; unemployment stays at the 6% natural rate.

answers.brief_reasoning: When workers expect higher inflation, they build it into wage contracts and firms build it into prices. This raises production costs and shifts SRAS left. As a result, every unemployment rate now comes with a higher inflation rate.
answers.final_answer: Higher expected inflation leads workers to demand higher nominal wages and firms to raise prices. Costs rise (SRAS shifts left), so each unemployment rate is paired with higher inflation and the SRPC shifts up.

answers.brief_reasoning: A higher real interest rate means less private investment. This is crowding out.
answers.final_answer: Private investment spending decreases

answers.brief_reasoning: Borrowing costs more, so fewer investment projects have an expected return above the real interest rate.
answers.final_answer: The higher real interest rate raises the cost of borrowing, so firms borrow less and fund fewer capital projects. Private investment falls (crowding out).

answers.brief_reasoning: Lower investment means less capital is built up, so productivity grows more slowly.
answers.final_answer: Less private investment slows growth of the capital stock, which slows productivity growth and long-run economic growth (the LRAS/PPC shifts right more slowly)

content.text:
Country A's OC of 1 laptop = 60/120 = 0.5 bicycle. B: 60/60 = 1 bicycle. A has comparative advantage in laptops.

PPC: A intercepts laptops 120 (horizontal), bicycles 60 (vertical). Tech doubles bicycles: vertical intercept goes to 120, horizontal intercept stays at 120, so the line pivots outward.

D: specialize per comparative advantage; trade at terms between 0.5 and 1 bicycle per laptop.

answers.brief_reasoning: 60 bicycles / 120 laptops
answers.final_answer: 0.5 bicycle per laptop (60/120)

answers.brief_reasoning: A's OC 0.5 bicycle < B's OC 1 bicycle
answers.final_answer: Country A

answers.brief_reasoning: Straight-line PPC from (0 laptops,60 bicycles) to (120 laptops,0). After the tech advance, the bicycle intercept rises to 120 and the laptop intercept stays at 120, so the curve pivots outward along the bicycle axis.
answers.final_answer: Original PPC: straight line with intercepts of 60 bicycles (vertical axis) and 120 laptops (horizontal axis). New PPC2: pivots outward to 120 bicycles on the vertical axis, with the laptop intercept unchanged at 120.

answers.brief_reasoning: Specialize by comparative advantage, then trade at terms between the two opportunity costs
answers.final_answer: A specializes in laptops (OC 0.5 bicycle) and B in bicycles (OC 1 laptop per bicycle, lower than A's 2). Both then trade at terms between 0.5 and 1 bicycle per laptop, e.g. 0.75 bicycle per laptop. This lets each country consume beyond its own PPC.

answers.brief_reasoning: AD shifts right to AD2 and crosses SRAS at YF. Along an upward-sloping SRAS this gives a higher price level PL2 > PL1. But the stimulus says the price level stays constant when spending changes, so PL2 should equal PL1. Also, if prices do rise, $16B would not fully close the gap.
answers.final_answer: AD2 lies to the right of AD1 and crosses SRAS at YF, with PL2 above PL1.
answers.flaw_note: This part conflicts with the stimulus. The stimulus says the price level is constant, which is what makes the $16B answer in part D work, yet this part asks for a new, higher PL2. If prices rise, the simple multiplier overstates the output gain.
